verdict.rationale: The lexical engine has two reinforcing parts. Positive: Gen 2:24 builds the cleaving and one-flesh formula from davaq (H1692) plus basar (H1320) plus echad (H0259), and that exact formula is quoted at Matt 19:5, 1 Cor 6:16, and Eph 5:31, locating one-flesh union inside the man-and-wife pair. Heb 13:4 sets the standing as timios ho gamos en pasin kai he koite amiantos (G1062, G2845, G0283), the marriage bed alone honored and undefiled. Negative: porneia (G4202, 26 NT occurrences) is the broad lexical category for illicit sexual intercourse and is the explicit object of prohibition (1 Cor 6:18 pheugete ten porneian, 1 Thess 4:3 apechesthai apo tes porneias, Eph 5:3 mede onomazestho), with porneuo verb form (G4203), pornos noun (G4205), porne noun (G4204). Heb 13:4 names pornous separately from moichous (G3432), so porneia is not narrowed to adultery. The OT cognate zanah (H2181, 91 occurrences) plus the betulim virginity case in Deut 22:14, 20-21 plus the seduction case in Exod 22:16 give an unbroken OT-to-NT pattern that brackets sexual relations inside marriage and labels intercourse outside it as wrong.

scripture.force: The foundational clause says a man leaves father and mother, cleaves (davaq, H1692) to his wife, and the two become one flesh (basar echad, H1320 plus H0259). The verb davaq paired with basar echad makes the one-flesh union an attribute of the husband-wife pair specifically, not of any sexual partnership. Matt 19:5, 1 Cor 6:16, and Eph 5:31 cite this verse with kollaomai and proskollao plus sarx, transferring the same boundary into the NT.

Deut 22:20-21 makes the absence of betulim (virginity-tokens, H1331) at marriage prosecutable, and characterizes the act as zanah (H2181, to act as a prostitute or commit sexual immorality) committed in the father's house before marriage. The case law therefore explicitly classes premarital sex by an unmarried woman as zanah, the OT cognate of porneia.

Timios ho gamos en pasin kai he koite amiantos, pornous gar kai moichous krinei ho theos. Marriage (gamos) is honorable and the bed (koite) undefiled (amiantos), bounded by gamos itself, and God will judge pornous and moichous. Listing pornous separately from moichous lexically distinguishes sexual immorality (including non-adulterous fornication) from adultery, so porneia is not narrowed to adultery alone.

Ho kollomenos te porne hen soma estin. He cites Gen 2:24, esontai gar phesin hoi duo eis sarka mian, to argue that joining to a porne (sexual partner outside marriage) creates the one-flesh bond, but in the wrong place. The argument only works if one-flesh union is by lexical definition the husband-wife bond, so sexual joining outside marriage misuses the union.

Pheugete ten porneian. Pan hamartema ho ean poiese anthropos ektos tou somatos estin, ho de porneuon eis to idion soma hamartanei. The imperative is unrestricted (flee porneia), and the participle ho porneuon (the one committing porneia) is described as sinning against his own body, with no carve-out for an unmarried participant.

Dia de tas porneias hekastos ten heautou gynaika echeto kai hekaste ton idion andra echeto. The remedy for porneia is for each man to have his own wife and each woman her own husband, naming gyne and aner as the licit channel for sexual relations. The reasoning presupposes that sexual relations outside that pair count as porneia.

Touto gar estin thelema tou theou, ho hagiasmos hymon, apechesthai hymas apo tes porneias. God's will is identified with hagiasmos, identified in turn with abstaining from porneia. The genitive tes porneias is the unqualified category of illicit sexual intercourse.

Eidenai hekaston hymon to heautou skeuos ktasthai en hagiasmo kai time. Each is to know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor, paired with the contrast in v. 5 me en pathei epithymias kathaper kai ta ethne, that is, not in the passion of lust like the nations. The vocabulary heautou skeuos plus hagiasmos plus time matches the marriage-bed honor formula of Heb 13:4.

Me en pathei epithymias kathaper kai ta ethne ta me eidota ton theon. The believer's conduct is set against pathos epithymias, the passion of lust, characteristic of the nations who do not know God. The lexical opposition places unregulated sexual desire outside the sanctified pattern.

Porneia de kai akatharsia pasa e pleonexia mede onomazestho en hymin. Porneia and all impurity must not even be named among the saints, an emphatic prohibition that treats porneia as wholly outside the believing community's life.

Anti toutou kataleipsei anthropos ton patera kai ten metera kai proskollethesetai pros ten gynaika autou, kai esontai hoi duo eis sarka mian. Paul restates Gen 2:24 in connection with husband and wife, fixing the one-flesh bond as the marital bond and providing the NT lexical anchor for the husband-wife scope of sexual union.

complicating_texts.resolution: Exod 22:16-17 sets the case of a man seducing an unbetrothed virgin: the resolution is that he must pay the mohar (bride-price) and marry her, or pay the bride-price if her father refuses. The case treats the act as a wrong requiring restitution and channels the relation into marriage. It does not treat unmarried sex as morally indifferent. It treats it as a sexual offense whose remedy is to constitute the marriage the act anticipated.

Deut 22:28-29 sets the same kind of case (unbetrothed virgin) with mandatory marriage and a fine, again channeling the act into marriage rather than treating it as licit. The vocabulary of taphas and shakab marks the intercourse, and the requirement to marry signals that the relation was meant to be marital.

Patriarchal narratives (Abraham with Hagar, Jacob with Bilhah and Zilpah) record concubinage and surrogate-bearing arrangements. The narrative records these arrangements without lexically endorsing them, and the prophetic and torah vocabulary (zanah, betulim, naaph) continues to bracket sexual relations inside the man-wife pair. Genre is descriptive narrative not legal warrant.

The interpretive crux at 1 Cor 7:36-38 concerns either a father-of-a-virgin reading or a betrothed-couple reading. On either reading the resolution is to marry (gameitosan), which keeps the licit channel for sexual relations inside gamos. The lexical pattern of the doctrine is unaffected.

variants.note: No variant units were supplied in the bundle. The marginal gar in Heb 13:4 and the bracketed pasa in Eph 5:3 are minor and do not touch the load-bearing terms porneia, koite, amiantos, hamartanei, gamos, or pornos. The 1 Cor 7:36-38 textual issues affect the referent of the parthenos but not the imperative to marry. These NT epistles fall outside the published CBGM scope, hence ecm-shadow.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reading porneia as the standing broad category of illicit sexual intercourse (its range includes the incest of 1 Cor 5:1, prostitution of 1 Cor 6:16, and the general category in 1 Thess 4:3 and Eph 5:3), combined with the Gen 2:24 one-flesh formula cited at Matt 19:5, 1 Cor 6:16, and Eph 5:31, yields a verdict that sexual relations are reserved for the husband-wife pair and that pre-marital and non-marital sexual union falls under porneia.

Even if porneia were read narrowly in some contexts (cult prostitution, incest, or sex with prostitutes specifically), the positive boundary remains: gamos is honorable and koite amiantos (Heb 13:4), the one-flesh formula in Gen 2:24 is restricted to a man and his wife, and 1 Cor 7:2 names a man's own wife and a woman's own husband as the remedy for porneia. The marriage-bed boundary stands even on a narrow reading of porneia.

Some readers note that the OT case law in Exod 22:16-17 and Deut 22:28-29 envisions the sexual act constituting or anticipating marriage rather than being free of consequence. Stated in its strongest form, this lens still classifies the unmarried sexual act as a sexual offense requiring formal marriage and bride-price, never as morally neutral. The proposition that sex is reserved for marriage is preserved.

On a redemptive-historical reading, the OT permits some practices (polygamy, concubinage in patriarchal narrative) that the NT does not endorse, and the NT consolidates sexual ethics around the Gen 2:24 monogamous pair (Matt 19:5, 1 Cor 7:2, Eph 5:31). The trajectory tightens, never loosens, the boundary around sex inside the husband-wife pair, so the verdict holds across the canonical arc.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict rests on two pillars that converge: the standing semantic range of porneia plus its OT cognate zanah, and the Gen 2:24 one-flesh formula cited three times in the NT. analogia_scripturae is engaged because 1 Cor 7:2 supplies the licit channel (gyne, aner) that the prohibition presupposes. progressive_revelation is engaged because the NT tightens the one-flesh formula to a single husband-wife pair while OT narrative tolerated practices the NT does not endorse.

stem_audit.notes: The stem labels pre-marital sex and sexual cohabitation as sin. This is the lexical conclusion of the cited terms rather than a tradition-specific taxonomy: the word sin tracks hamartanei and hamartema in 1 Cor 6:18, abstention tracks apechesthai apo tes porneias in 1 Thess 4:3, the OT case law uses zanah (H2181) in Deut 22:21, and the marriage boundary tracks gamos plus koite amiantos in Heb 13:4 plus the Gen 2:24 one-flesh formula. The parenthetical gloss fornication for porneia is a standard lexical equivalence, not a loaded framing, so no neutralization is required.

lay_summary: Two lexical pillars carry this question. The first is the Greek word porneia, which appears 26 times in the New Testament as the broad term for illicit sexual intercourse. In 1 Corinthians 6:18 the command is to flee porneia, and the one who commits it is said to sin against his own body, using the verb hamartanei. In 1 Thessalonians 4:3 God's will, called sanctification, is to abstain from porneia. In Ephesians 5:3 porneia and all impurity must not even be named among the saints. Hebrews 13:4 lists pornous (the sexually immoral) separately from moichous (adulterers), so porneia is not narrowed to married people straying. Its Old Testament cognate, the Hebrew zanah, appears 91 times, and Deuteronomy 22:20-21 uses it for sexual relations by an unmarried woman before marriage, treating the absence of virginity-tokens as a punishable wrong. The second pillar is positive. Genesis 2:24 says a man leaves father and mother, cleaves (davaq) to his wife, and the two become one flesh (basar echad). That clause is cited three times in the New Testament, by Jesus at Matthew 19:5, by Paul at 1 Corinthians 6:16 (where joining to a prostitute is wrong because it misplaces the one-flesh bond), and by Paul at Ephesians 5:31. Hebrews 13:4 puts the same point as a standing: marriage, gamos, is honorable and the bed, he koite, is undefiled, amiantos, bounded by marriage itself. 1 Corinthians 7:2 names a man's own wife and a woman's own husband as the remedy for porneia. Where readers diverge, it tends to be over the exact width of porneia or whether the Old Testament case law in Exodus 22:16 and Deuteronomy 22:28 treats unmarried sex as a wrong remedied by marriage or as constituting marriage. Even on the narrower readings, the words still locate sexual union inside the husband-wife pair and treat sexual activity outside it as a sexual offense.
